newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - MBS vs corps? US managers split for 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - MBS vs corps? US managers split for 1997.

text.p: While many total return fixed-income managers expect a healthy U.S. bond market in 1997, players disagree on which of the two main sectors of spread product -- mortgage-backed securities (MBS) or corporate bonds -- will perform better.

Peter McTeague, strategist at MCM Moneywatch, noted as the new year approaches, "People who are bullish on bonds are staying away from mortgages. Those who believe bonds will be range-bound are looking for the beaten dogs of the last few months. Mortgages are one of those products."
MORTGAGE-BACKED SECURITIES

Going into the new year, money managers were torn between their desire for the juicy yields of MBS relative to corporates and fear that continued interest rates declines would cause MBS to underperform.

Bill Stevens, senior portfolio manager for Montgomery Fixed-Income Funds, is overweighting MBS becuase he believes interest rates will be range-bound in 1997. In this environment, higher-yielding MBS will outperform corporates, he said.
Stevens acknowledged his concerns about the downside risk to MBS in the case of a substantial prepayment pickup.

"The next 50 basis point drop (in market interest rates) will generate much more press focus on refinancing opportunities and more people will pay attention. Prepayments are at risk of going up a lot more," he said.

Nevertheless, given his rate forecast, Stevens is willing to overweight premium and slight-premium coupon MBS, which are more susceptible to a prepayment pickup. He noted these bonds are trading at cheaper levels following the recent rally in interest rates.

On the other hand, Wayne Lyski, head of fixed-income at Alliance Capital Management, said he expects long-term rates to drop substanitally in 1997 and is maintaining only a market weighting in the sector.
"I don't think mortgages offer an extraordinary value if you have a bullish orientation," he said.
"If the long-bond (yield) goes down to six percent and the 10-year falls to 5 3/4 percent, I think you will run the risk of another prepayment wave," he added.
Lyski is leaning toward discount- and current-coupon MBS, which would tend to outperform higher-coupon MBS products in a rallying market environment.
"We have our finger on the trigger to reduce exposure if rates turn down," he added.
Joe Balestrino, portfolio manager at Federated Investors, said his firm was also emphasizing current- and discount-coupon MBS.
"The economy has seen its best days go by and that means rates will be falling. One has to add convexity and quality in this environment," Balestrino said.
CORPORATES
Bond managers expressed frustration that spreads on investment-grade and high-yield corporate bonds remain close to historically tight levels.
Federated's Balestrino, who fears an economic slowdown, viewed such rich price levels as a warning that corporates, particularly those of weaker credit quality, were becoming riskier to own.
"We have been upgrading the credit quality of our portfolio. While we are giving up some income, we think that when you have a spread-widening wave, we will outperform," he said.
Balestrino said he has been swapping single-B-rated bonds, with more exposure to credit risk, for double-B rated bonds that are more interest-rate sensitive.
"We are looking for double-Bs that may have potential, even in a slowing economy, to be upgraded," he added.
"I would pick credits like Oryx Energy Co, a double-B rated oil and gas company, and Federated Department Stores Inc, a triple-B-rated bond." Both have potential for rating upgrades, he said.
Balestrino said he has also been de-emphasizing cyclical credits and overweighting sectors with long-term growth potential like telecommunications and media sector bonds.
Peter Van Dyke, head of taxable fixed-income at T. Rowe Price Associates, said most areas of the corporate bond market look too rich relative to MBS, particularly in the short-end of the yield curve.

"The one area in corporates that we will like is financials. Domestic and Yankee bank paper is attractive. Banks have their balance sheets in order and are even getting cautious about consumer loans," Van Dyke said.
Van Dyke likes Union Planters Corp. and Chase Manhattan Corp. bonds in particular, saying both banks are candidates for potential rating upgrades.

In stark contrast to Van Dyke and Balestrino, Alliance's Lyski, who has a more bullish outlook on the economy and interest rates, said his main focus this year will continue to be on high-yielding, lower-rated bonds.

"The greater credit risk you can take, the better off you will be in 1997," Lyski said. "More growth will allow emerging markets to continue to restructure their economies and domestic corporations to continue to improve their balance sheets."
Lyski acknowledged many credits in the high-yield and emerging market sectors are fully valued, but he said opportunities still abound.

He particularly likes bonds from small emerging market countries such as Panama and Peru, which he said could both experience 50 to 75 basis points in spread tightening as their economies improve in 1997.
